items.text: AMEND AND RECOMMIT TO LOCAL GOVERNMENT
ORDERED TO THIRD READING RULES CAL.437

items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S4601

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the local finance law, in relation to bond
anticipation notes; to amend the local finance law, in relation to the
private sale of bonds; to amend the local finance law, in relation to
notice of sale of bonds; to amend the local finance law, in relation
to bid deposits for the public sale of bonds; to amend the local
finance law, in relation to authorizing municipalities, school
districts and district corporations to issue deficiency notes; and
providing for the repeal of certain provisions upon expiration thereof


 PURPOSE :

This bill proposes to: extend the "roll over" period for bond
anticipation notes; increase the cap from one million dollars to five
million dollars for allowing certain bonds to be sold at private sale
without limitation as to rate of interest; shorten the minimum notice
of a change in the time or date for the opening of certain bids from
24 hours to 1 hour prior to the time originally scheduled for the
opening of bids; allow cash remitted by wire transfer to a specified
account to be furnished as security as a condition precedent to the
consideration of a bidders bid; and allow a municipality, school
district or district corporation to issue deficiency notes during any
fiscal year to finance a deficiency in any fund or funds arising from
revenues being less than the amount estimated in the budget for the
current fiscal year.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of this bill would amend paragraph b of section 23.00 of the
Local Finance Law to allow bond anticipation notes issued originally'
during calendar year 2004 or 2005 to extend as far as seven years
beyond their original date of issue.

Sections 2, 3, 4 and 5 of this bill would amend subdivision 5 of
paragraph d of section 57.00, paragraphs a and b of section 62.10, and
the section heading and paragraphs a and b of section 63.00 of the
Local Finance Law to increase the current $1,000,000 cap on negotiated
sales and/or modify the requirements under which local governments can
apply for a waiver from competitive sale in certain market conditions.

Section 6 of this bill requires a report by the State Comptroller on
the private sales of bonds conducted pursuant to paragraph b of
section 63.00 of the Local Finance Law.

Section 7 of this bill would amend subparagraphs (b) and (d) of
subdivision 2 of paragraph b of section 58.00 of the Local Finance Law
to modify the current cancellation of notice of sale requirement.

Sections 8 and 9 of this bill would amend subdivision 3 of paragraph c
of section 58.00 and paragraph c of section 59.00 of the Local Finance
Law to expand options for good faith deposits to include cash.

Sections 10, 11, 12 and 13 of this bill would amend section 10.00 and
subdivision 40 of paragraph a of section 11.00 of the Local Finance
Law and add two new sections 29.20 and 40.10 to the Local Finance Law
to permit budget notes for revenue shortfalls.

Section 14 of this bill states this act is effective immediately.

 JUSTIFICATION :

This bill has 5 main objectives:
1) Except in the case of bond anticipation notes issued for
"assessable improvements" (e.g., town water or sewer projects), local
governments are authorized to extend or "roll over" bond anticipation
notes for only up to 5 years. At the end of that period, the bond
anticipation notes must be retired or converted into long-term debt.
Extending the "roll over" period by 2 years would create another
option for a municipality currently faced with maturing bond
anticipation notes, particularly in this volatile market environment.
The grant of authority would be temporary (with a "sunset" provision)
so that it would be re-evaluated as market conditions change in the
future. Similar grants of authority were enacted in the 1970s and
1980s. The State's Short Term Investment Pool (S TIP) can also playa
role in potentially purchasing bond anticipation notes (BANs), tax
anticipation notes (TANs) or revenue anticipation notes (RANS) when a
local government issuer lacks market access. Under current law
(subject to certain exceptions), localities may only sell bonds
totaling $1 million or less on a negotiated basis. One of the
exceptions is for bonds sold at a discount, subject to the
Comptroller's approval. Under Office of the State Comptroller
Regulations, a local government may sell discount bonds at negotiated
sale with the Comptroller's approval if it has determined that a
competitive sale is expected to produce higher borrowing costs and is
not in the best interests of the issuers because of (1) unstable or
volatile market conditions, (2) conditions of fiscal stress or
negative credit factors experienced by the issuer, (3) the large
dollar amount of the proposed issuance, or (4) the complexity of the
issue.

2) Financial advisors and underwriters often favor negotiated sales in
a volatile market environment because buyers are lined up in advance
of the sale. Several recent competitive sales by NYS local governments
have attracted only one or two bidders.  Local governments,
particularly those with lower credit ratings, may benefit if the
threshold was increased or conditions for waiver were modified.
Consideration should be given to increasing the threshold and to
expanding the negotiated sale exception to other than discount bonds,
subject to the factors in Office of the State Comptroller regulations.
However, the Office of the State Comptroller has traditionally favored
competitive bond sales as a more cost-efficient method of financing
both on the State and local level, and a local government waiver
modification creates potential staff workload issues to address a
potential influx of waivers.

3) Local governments are required to provide at least 24 hours notice
if a sale is cancelled or if the sale date is changed. Given
technology, this provision could be modified to allow local
governments to cancel or postpone a sale up to one hour before pricing
on the day of sale. This change would allow a municipal issuer to
evaluate market conditions on the day of the planned sale to determine
whether the sale is likely to be successful.

4) Bidders are required to deposit at least 1 percent of the total
amount of bonds desired via cashiers or certified check (or eligible
surety bond) as a "good faith effort" in a competitive bond sale.
This protects the local government should the low bidder end up not
purchasing the bonds. This requirement should be modified to allow for
cash deposits via wire transfer. In addition, if the notice of sale
provision is modified, this requirement could also be modified to a
lower percentage to help mitigate any purchaser liquidity concerns.

5) Currently, local governments are authorized to issue budget notes
to finance certain unforeseeable emergencies and situations where
there is insufficient appropriation authority. There is no analogous
authority to issue short term notes in the case of an unforeseen
revenue shortfall. Consideration should be given to modifying the
Local Finance Law for this event. The issuance of budget notes would
help local governments respond to unforeseen budget problems and could
obviate their need to seek a special act for deficit financing for
relatively small, one-time shortfalls.

The Comptroller urges passage of this legislation.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New Proposal.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :

Immediately.
